I am absolutely astonished at how ugly this movie is. I complained that the 2005 one had lots of bad CG, but oh my god it’s maybe even worse here almost two decades later and there’s wayyyy more of it just constantly. It’s so bad that I was genuinely wondering at times if some of the effects were AI generated. Amidst all the bad greenscreen and CGI is the occasional physical prop or set, which look so cheap you’d think these specialized props were purchased at Spirit Halloween. And as if that’s not bad enough, the whole movie has this gross filter that takes all the color out and makes it look gray and dull and terrible. I hate it I hate it I hate it, not one fucking frame of this movie looks even somewhat okay to the point that it made me actually angry while watching. I could genuinely complain about it so much more, I would rate this at least a full star higher if it wasn’t one of the ugliest movies I’ve ever seen in my entire life. The plot of this movie is real basic and predictable but not bad. The cast is all pretty good, I was not really expecting to like Timothee Chalamet as Wonka but I honestly did. There’s some good music but some of the songs are kinda boring and go on longer than they need to. The humor is mixed with some genuinely funny jokes and some really obnoxious bad comedy. Le film de Paul King sur le biopic de Wonka est une oeuvre orienté jeunesse. On sens une très grande inspiration cartoon de NOS jeunes années. Les chansons et danses omniprésentes parlent d'eux même mais ne sont pas les seuls points caractérisant ce coté cartoons. Les cadrages et décors colorés rappellent des prises de vue non habituelle du cinéma et une autre facon de retourner dans notre enfance. Le scénario va de paire avec cette idée, pas très elaboré ni très originale, cependant efficace. Le seul point noir de ce film est sa pâte graphique. Quelques manques de qualité de 3D se font ressentir. Surtout lors de deux scenes, les bonbons volants et la scène final de la fabrique. Malgré tout la girafe CGI fait très bien son effet. C'est avec plaisir que j'ai vu ce film de Paul King qui m'a encore renvoyé en enfance après ma découverte de ce réalisateur avec les deux films Paddington qui m'ont émerveillé.

wasn’t put on in work it probably wouldn’t of been one I was watching any time soon, However within a minute of this being put on I was hooked, drawn to the screen by the energetic performance of Timothée Chalamet, he’s probably my favourite young actor today and he brings to life the energy and charisma of Willy Wonka just like those who have come before, it’s not just Chalamet who holds up his end of the bargain either, everyone holds there own in this film through there magical performances and looking a the cast list it’s not hard to see why, but as a Brit who loves Peep Show I’ve got to give a special mention to Paterson Joseph, his role as Johnson is my favourite in Peep Show, he’s electric in every role I’ve seen him in and often steals the show, he goes toe to toe with the eccentric Wonka as the evil businessman Slugworth and I’d be lying if there both not as good as each other here, But even if the performances and whimsical world of Roald Dahl isn’t enough to sell you this movie breezes by you with its fun nature, I said to the people in work it boils down really to a serious crime/thriller movie for families, Wonka trying to take and supply on the Businessmen Turf with great music and perfectly capturing the spirit and childhood imagination that all good Roald Dahl stories/worlds have, Chalamet oozes out the seems in the role of Wonka and it would be a crime if we never got to see him portray the role again, the rest of the cast hold there own and it wears its heart and emotions on it sleeves, colourful and dreamy yet serious when it needs to be, Wonka is a ‘Tis the season for a sweet treat and, whilst not anything to do with Christmas, Wonka hits quite a lot of the festive buttons: fun, light-hearted, colourful and one for all the family. With much of the Paddington team behind this, it delivers that quintessentially English, quirky family film that its forebear (pun intended) achieved but sprinkled with a little bit of Cruella in its prequel backstory to a familiar character. It doesn’t present the titular chocolatier as a villain though, and rubs maybe just a little too much mystery off of the character, but does still feel very much a Roald Dahl tale. Wonka’s dream is to open a chocolate shop and he arrives in an alt-Paris (I think it’s meant to be Paris) to compete against the most famous chocolate makers of the time. From there, frolics, mishaps and big musical numbers ensue. Yes, this is a full musical like the OG Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory. Taking a couple of the songs but throwing in some excellent originals, this could well be destined for a stage run itself in the future. It’s cut through with a particularly English sense of humour and a brilliant ‘spot the famous person’ cast with a, hopefully intended, hat tip to Peep Show and yet another turn from Hugh Grant’s new comedy persona as an Oompa-Loompa. It’s just an utter delight, against all the odds, much like the aforementioned Cruella. A brisk and breezy one-for-all-the-family movie to smack a smile on your face. ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️

I had a genuinely good time with Wonka . It’s bright, energetic, and packed with colourful spectacle that mostly works. The musical numbers are catchy, the production design is playful, and there’s an infectious sense of fun running through a lot of it. For pure candy-coated entertainment, it delivers. And yet something about it never quite sat right. The pacing is uneven. The film often feels like it’s rushing through its own plot points or lingering a little too long on moments that don’t land with the weight they need. The whimsy is constant, which is part of the charm, but it also starts to feel one-note. The story never really digs under the surface of its own confectionery. Timothée Chalamet is a strange fit for young Willy Wonka. He has the ethereal, slightly otherworldly quality that could theoretically work, and he commits fully, but the performance never fully convinced me. There’s a lightness and a calculated eccentricity that sometimes feels more like an actor playing at being Wonka than someone who could grow into the strange, controlling, faintly menacing figure we know from the books and earlier films. The casting choice is stylish, but it leaves a gap where a more unsettling presence might have been. What’s most noticeable is the absence of any real darkness. Classic Wonka has always had a sharp edge under the sugar—an air of the sinister, the punitive, the slightly unhinged. This film largely sands that away in favour of pure optimism and adventure. It’s enjoyable on its own terms, but it leaves the character feeling incomplete. That’s why the news of a sequel is interesting. I hope the next film is willing to lean into the stranger, colder side of Wonka. I want to see the cracks form. I want the story of how the charming inventor becomes someone capable of the more ruthless, almost cruel decisions later associated with him. The origin of that shift—whatever mixture of betrayal, isolation, obsession, or quiet bitterness drives it—is the version of the character I’m still waiting for. Wonka is a fun, colourful ride. I just left wanting the shadow as well as the light.
